baseline_mismatch.observation: Native succeeds at retained index0 with wrapped zero stride; baseline Rust panics in require_element_stride before invoking the constructor.
baseline_mismatch.red_scope: The initial two-test target preceded later scenario additions and helper formatting; red log is historical regression evidence, not a claim that all final cases ran against baseline.

cumulative_review.selection_reason: Existing constructor arithmetic preserves increment0 metadata and protected raw allocation wrapping, but public append/access/erase still blanket-rejected all zero-stride use. Native retained first-slot lifecycle is defined without new allocation and does not require sparse initialized-slot ownership. Existing cached adapters are not duplicated.

behavior: Routes append through a shared physical-location preparation step. Nonzero stride retains existing block growth; zero stride requires used0, nonzero-sized T, a retained first block with capacity>0 and no registered value in slot0 before any callback. Successful first-slot construction performs no block/table growth, then publishes used1 and marks the conservative initialized-tail scan.

Element access uses native zero-stride coordinates (block=index,offset=index), then checks actual registered initialized lengths before forming references. First/Last and unsigned/signed Value conveniences can access the live first slot. Removed or unregistered values remain outside safe reference access even if their bytes survive.

Both ordinary EraseLast and the existing scoped destructor adapter accept the one registered first-slot state. The explicit adapter preserves original-slot destruction and callback-time used1; native noexcept parity still requires no unwind. Rust-only panic recovery removes ownership and decrements size without automatic double destruction.

Clear at zero stride runs no element destructors, matching the native aCount0 formula. It sets each typed block initialized length to0 without moving bytes, then retains or releases physical blocks according to the existing flag. This deliberately abandons cleanup obligations rather than silently running Rust Drop. Normal positive-stride destruction order is unchanged.

Nineteen native UBSan rows establish stable retained first-slot identity, Value/ChangeValue/First/Last, EraseLast destruction, Clear(false/true) omission, explicit destructor repair while storage remains alive, stride-reset reuse, borrowed/moved/default Append paths, active SetIncrement no-op, empty/freed storage and reset recovery, and constructor throw/retry state.

Native std::shared_ptr and Rust Rc payloads demonstrate an unreleased strong owner after Clear(false): strong_count remains1 until test-only in-place repair makes it0. Strict Miri executes this ownership repair without leaking the resource or dereferencing freed storage. Clear(true) omission is observed with a non-heap-owning destructor counter; no repair through freed storage is attempted.

Nine integration regressions and two units cover the native rows, missing/freed storage, later sparse index rejection before callback or metadata mutation, actual owned-slot checks, scoped erase observation/unwind, cached zero-stride rejection, scan gating and invalid erasure metadata. All52 original runtime names join normal and strict Miri logs.

Twelve exact native declaration IDs bind13 current body-bearing public Rust methods. The duplicate EmplaceAppend template/child rows and shared generic Value bindings are explicit; no global legacy/API completion credit is added.
limitations: Later zero-stride appends can have defined native targets when enough retained blocks and per-block capacity exist: native indexi selects blocki,offseti. This implementation rejects them before construction because AllocVec registered prefixes cannot represent those sparse diagonal live slots without a broader ownership model. They remain actionable parity gaps, not blanket native UB.

Zero-stride SetValue/EmplaceValue/Insert paths, default-constructing mutable IndexMut access and cached iterator capture still require separate work. The cached engine continues rejecting zero stride, with explicit regression coverage; no pointer/cursor parity claim was silently broadened.

After Clear(false), omitted objects may remain live in retained bytes, but safe Rust access rejects them because automatic ownership was relinquished. Caller-owned unsafe raw access/repair needs live allocation, initialization, lifetime and exclusivity proofs. Clear(true) ends storage lifetime; freed pointers must never be repaired or read.

Ordinary EraseLast keeps its existing convenience metadata timing; the unsafe scoped erase adapter supplies native callback-time Size. Native destroyAt is noexcept, whereas the tested Rust panic-recovery path is an extension and is not native throw equivalence.

Zero-sized T, later sparse initialization, incompatible layout/allocator ownership, unpublished raw lifetimes, arbitrary C++ trait inference and constructor-failure resource/descriptor lifetime differences remain partial. The one-slot path checks actual typed capacity and never treats a zero-byte raw request as valid typed element storage.

The native probe uses pinned x86_64 unsigned wrapping behavior and prebuilt TKernel under a UBSan-instrumented fixture. API receipts in files whose hashes changed remain historical snapshots; this receipt captures new bodies and does not rewrite the shared parity ledger.
validation_scope: 307 integration tests across24 DynamicArray targets,23 units,120 strict Miri tests,52 original native tests,19 UBSan fixture rows,fmt,strict scoped Clippy and compiler extraction. Bounded retained index0 lifecycle only; no full zero-stride or class completion claim.
